en.name: Preserved lemons
en.summary: Preserved lemons are whole lemons packed in salt and cured in their own juice until the peel goes soft and translucent. Refrigerated in their brine they keep about 4–6 months, provided the fruit stays submerged and surface scum is skimmed. The cupboard is the traditional practice but not one any food-safety authority endorses.
en.pantry: A cupboard jar is the traditional Moroccan practice and how most recipes are written, but it is not a practice any food-safety authority endorses for the home, and no defensible number can be given for it — which is why none appears here. The cure itself does need room temperature: leave the jar out for roughly three to four weeks, turning it daily so the salt and juice reach everything. After that, the refrigerator is where the jar should live.
en.fridge: Keep the jar at 4 °C (40 °F) or below, where about 4–6 months is the range — the figure published for fully fermented pickles, which preserved lemons are a salt-cured example of, and it comes with the same two conditions. First, keep the fruit pushed under the brine; a lemon standing proud of the liquid is where mould starts. Second, skim any surface scum whenever you open the jar. Use a clean dry fork, never fingers. The brine goes syrupy and the peel goes translucent and soft over the first weeks of curing — that is the cure working, not spoilage.
en.freezer: There is no freezer timeline for preserved lemons and freezing is beside the point: salt is already doing the preserving, and months in the fridge is longer than most cooks take to use a jar. If you have chopped more peel than a recipe needs, freezing small portions of the chopped peel is reasonable, but the whole fruit is better left in its brine where it goes on improving.
spoilage: Fuzzy or coloured mould, especially on fruit standing above the brine
Brine gone ropy, slimy or foul-smelling rather than thick and syrupy
A rotten or yeasty smell instead of a clean salty-citrus one
Flesh and peel collapsing into sludge rather than staying intact and soft
tips: Never cut back the salt in the recipe; the salt level is what makes it safe, not a seasoning choice.
Push the lemons back under the brine every time you open the jar.
Use a clean dry fork and keep water out.
Rinse a wedge before using it, and use the peel rather than the pulp in most dishes.

faq.q: How long do preserved lemons last?
faq.a: About 4–6 months refrigerated in their brine, as long as the fruit stays submerged and surface scum is removed regularly.

faq.q: Can you keep preserved lemons in the cupboard?
faq.a: That is the traditional practice, but no food-safety authority endorses it for the home and no defensible timeline can be given. Cure at room temperature, then refrigerate.

faq.q: Can you use less salt in preserved lemons?
faq.a: No. Do not cut back the salt a recipe requires — it is the preservative, not a seasoning.

faq.q: Is the white film on the brine a problem?
faq.a: Skim any surface scum whenever you open the jar. Fuzzy coloured mould, or a rotten smell, means the jar goes out.

zh.name: 鹽漬檸檬
zh.summary: 鹽漬檸檬是把整顆檸檬用大量鹽醃、泡在自己的汁液裡熟成，直到果皮變軟、變透明。連同醃汁冷藏大約 4～6 個月，前提是果實要保持泡在液面下，並定期撈除表面浮沫。放櫥櫃是傳統做法，但沒有任何食品安全機關為家庭用途背書。
zh.pantry: 一罐放在櫥櫃是摩洛哥的傳統做法，多數食譜也是這樣寫的，但沒有任何食品安全機關為家庭用途背書，也給不出站得住腳的天數——所以這裡不給數字。熟成本身確實需要室溫：把罐子放在室溫大約三到四週，每天翻轉一次，讓鹽和汁液接觸到每一面。之後，這罐就該住進冰箱。
zh.fridge: 請放 4 °C 以下，大約 4～6 個月——這是「完全發酵醃漬品」公布的數字，而鹽漬檸檬正是這一類的鹽漬品，同時也附帶同樣的兩個條件。第一，讓果實保持壓在醃汁以下；露出液面的檸檬就是發霉的起點。第二，每次開罐都要撈掉表面浮沫。請用乾淨乾燥的叉子，不要用手。醃汁會變得濃稠、果皮會變透明變軟，那是熟成在進行，不是腐壞。
zh.freezer: 鹽漬檸檬沒有冷凍期限，冷凍也沒有意義：鹽已經在做保存的工作，而冷藏好幾個月，本來就比多數人用完一罐的時間長。如果切了比食譜需要更多的果皮，把切碎的果皮分小份冷凍是合理的；但整顆檸檬最好留在醃汁裡，它會愈放愈好。
spoilage: 長出毛狀或有顏色的霉，尤其在露出醃汁的果實上
醃汁變得牽絲、黏滑或有異味，而不是濃稠如糖漿
聞起來是腐敗味或酵母味，而不是乾淨的鹹味帶柑橘香
果肉和果皮爛成泥，而不是完整柔軟
tips: 絕對不要減少食譜裡的鹽量；鹽是防腐劑，不是調味選項。
每次開罐都把檸檬壓回醃汁裡。
用乾淨乾燥的叉子，不要讓水進去。
要用時先沖洗一瓣，多數料理用果皮而不是果肉。

faq.a: 連同醃汁冷藏大約 4～6 個月，前提是果實保持在液面下、表面浮沫定期撈除。

faq.q: 鹽漬檸檬可以放櫥櫃嗎？
faq.a: 那是傳統做法，但沒有食品安全機關為家庭用途背書，也給不出站得住腳的天數。請在室溫熟成後改為冷藏。

faq.q: 鹽漬檸檬可以少放鹽嗎？
faq.a: 不行。不要減少食譜要求的鹽量——鹽是防腐劑，不是調味。

faq.q: 醃汁上的白膜有問題嗎？
faq.a: 每次開罐把表面浮沫撈掉即可。但若是毛狀有顏色的霉，或有腐敗味，整罐就要丟掉。
